12.0.0.en: Zibiah: a woman from Beersheba, the wife of Ahaziah and the mother of Jehoash king of Judah.

12.0.1.en: Jehoash became king over Judah in the seventh year of Jehu king of Israel. His reign lasted forty years, and the capital of his kingdom was Jerusalem. The name of his mother was Zibiah, and she was from Beersheba. The name of his mother is mentioned out of concern and respect for this king, because of his good beginning.

12.1.0.en: Throughout the whole period in which Joash was under the guardianship of Jehoiada the priest, he did all that was right.

12.1.1.en: Seeking the help of spiritual guides leads a person to what pleases the Lord. So let us turn to our spiritual guides; they will light the way for us, that we may reach the harbor of safety. Let us not be proud and refuse to turn to them, lest we stray from the way of God.

12.2.0.en: But the problem of the high places remained, although the people sacrificed and offered burnt offerings not to pagan gods but to the true God, Jehovah.

12.2.1.en: In this there was a violation of the commandment, as we mentioned before, which had appointed one place, the Temple, for offering sacrifices.

12.2.2.en: Offering sacrifices on the high places was a ritual violation, that is, offering sacrifices in the wrong place, though not with the intention of worshiping idols. The first of the kings to introduce this idea was Solomon (1 Kgs 3:2-4). This led his son Rehoboam to fall into offering on the high places, not to God but to idols. Here the importance of obeying the Law appears, which protects us from turning away from God. The righteous kings of Judah, such as Asa and Jehoshaphat, were not able to remove worship on the high places (1 Kgs 15:14, 1 Kgs 22:43-44). As for the wicked ones, such as Abijam, Jehoram and Ahaziah, they worshiped idols. Then we come to the reign of Hezekiah, the righteous king, who was able to remove the high places and to prevent the offering of sacrifices on them, whether to God or to idols; but sadly they returned in the reign of his son Manasseh, and then Amon. Then there appeared the greatest of the kings of Judah, who walked like David in the worship of God, Josiah the righteous king, who not only removed the high places but also defiled them with the bones of the dead, so that none of the kings after him was able to worship on them.

12.3.0.en: Current silver: the silver in circulation.

12.3.1.en: The greatness and uprightness of Joash appear in his concern, before everything else, for the repair of the house of the Lord. He commanded the priests to collect the silver then in use, which was brought to the Temple in various ways, such as:

12.3.2.en: 1- What was offered for the souls of the people, which was half a shekel of silver (Ex 30:11-16).

12.3.3.en: 2- What was offered as the price of certain offerings, in place of them (Lev 27:11, 12).

12.3.5.en: And Joash commanded that this silver be used for the repair of the house of the Lord, which had fallen into ruin after being neglected in the days of the wicked kings Jehoram, Ahaziah and Athaliah, and especially Athaliah, who demolished parts of the Temple (2 Chr 24:7).

12.4.0.en: But the Temple remained unrepaired until the twenty-third year of the reign of Joash, because the priests collected the silver but took it for themselves and did not repair the Temple. They were not content to meet their needs from the silver, which the Law permits, but they took all the silver and neglected the repair of the house of the Lord and the carrying out of the king's orders, and this shows their love of money and their neglect of God.

12.4.1.en: Beware of the love of money, for it is the root of all evils. It begins with meeting your needs; then you become occupied with them and care about luxuries, and the luxuries become necessities without your realizing it, and your heart is taken up with money, so that your concern for the worship of God grows less. Hold to a spiritual rule in your relationship with God, in prayer, the Holy Bible, and a relationship with the sacraments and with repentance, so that you do not draw away from God without realizing it.

12.5.0.en: King Jehoash summoned Jehoiada the high priest together with the rest of the priests and rebuked them for not repairing the Temple. And he commanded them to take nothing of the silver coming into the house of the Lord, and consequently they would not be responsible for repairing the house of God. They agreed and obeyed him.

12.5.1.en: Here we see the vigilance of Joash in rebuking Jehoiada his teacher and all the priests under him. He had mastered what he learned from Jehoiada and held fast to it, even if Jehoiada himself was lax in his love and concern for the house of the Lord. We also find Joash taking up the responsibility for repairing the house of the Lord, since he would collect the silver and use it for the repair, apart from the priests.

12.5.2.en: Be vigilant and bear your responsibilities, even if others around you are lax, even if they are older than you; for you are responsible before God, and He is the One who will hold you to account and at the same time will help you, if you are diligent in your responsibilities before Him.

12.6.0.en: Jehoiada brought a chest, bored a hole in its lid, and set it at the right side of the altar of burnt offering, at the entrance of the Temple. The priests who kept the door put into it all the money that the contributors from the people brought for the house of the Lord. Here we see the cooperation of the priests and their concern to carry out the orders of King Joash, and perhaps this is due to two things:

12.6.1.en: 1- The priests were moved by the words of Joash and repented, because they had cared for their own needs more than for the house of the Lord, and so they expressed their repentance by putting the silver into the chest.

12.6.2.en: 2- Perhaps Jehoiada was moved, and at the same time rejoiced, at the words of his disciple King Joash, so he pressed the priests and commanded them to cooperate in carrying out the king's orders.

12.7.0.en: The great priest: he is Jehoiada.

12.7.1.en: They bound up and counted: they gathered the silver, which consisted of ingots of silver of fixed value that were known at that time, and they counted their value and put each amount in a bag of fixed value.

12.7.2.en: Whenever the chest was filled with silver, the committee formed of the king's scribe and the high priest would come to count the money inside it, to hand it over to the overseers appointed to supervise the work of repair, so that they might pay from it what was due to the carpenters and builders working on the repair, and also the masons, and buy the timber and stone and meet all the other costs of the repair.

12.7.3.en: From this we understand several things:

12.7.4.en: 1- The concern of Jehoiada and the king's trust in him. Although the king had reproached him, he trusted his faithfulness. If Jehoiada was lax in pressing the priests to take only what was necessary for their needs, he himself lived his simple life and was faithful in his personal life.

12.7.5.en: 2- His concern that there be a committee of two, so that none of the people would doubt the silver offered to the Temple, lest it be lost? This was especially so since one of the two, Jehoiada the high priest, was completely trusted.

12.7.6.en: 3- The Temple had suffered ruin, damage and neglect at the hands of many of the former kings, because of their preoccupation with the worship of Baal, so the repair of the Temple required a large number of workers skilled in the various branches of building.

12.8.0.en: Basins: wide vessels in which water or the blood of the sacrifices was put.

12.8.2.en: Bowls: small vessels for sprinkling blood.

12.8.3.en: The king and all those appointed by him gave priority to repairing the house of the Lord, and they spent none of the silver on completing the vessels and tools needed for the Temple, for this could be completed after making sure that the building was sound and complete. This shows the wisdom of the king and his orderly mind, and it also shows that the house lacked many of the vessels, because the former wicked kings had distributed the golden vessels of the Temple and given them to the enemies of the people of God (1 Kgs 14:26, 15:18). And after he finished the repair of the house, he also completed the vessels inside the Temple, as we understand from the Book of Chronicles (2 Chr 24:14).

12.9.0.en: These overseers appointed by the king were known for complete honesty in handling money, so he did not ask them to give an account of what they had spent on the work of repairing the Temple, since the work was very great and there was not time to submit accounts with all the details, and so they relied on their honesty. This shows the love and honesty of the people, which sometimes surpass those of the priests.

12.10.0.en: The just King Joash did not neglect the personal needs of the priests, and so he set aside for them the silver of the sin offering and the trespass offering. From this we see two things:

12.10.1.en: 1- The great blessing of the Lord when Joash gave attention to repairing the house, for the silver was plentiful, enough for the needs of the priests and the repair of the house.

12.10.2.en: 2- The priests' exaggeration in the past of their needs beyond what was fitting, as we mentioned earlier, before Joash commanded them to stop collecting the silver.

12.11.s.en: (3) The bribing of the king of Aram and then the death of Joash

12.11.0.en: Gath: one of the five great cities of the Philistines, lying south of the kingdom of Judah and near the Mediterranean Sea; it is an entrance to the kingdom of Judah.

12.11.2.en: Joash lived uprightly, worshiping God, all the life of Jehoiada the high priest. After the death of Jehoiada he was swayed by the words of the princes of Judah, as the Second Book of Chronicles tells us (2 Chr 24:15-21), and he forsook the Lord and worshiped idols. When Zechariah the priest, the son of Jehoiada, warned him, he was angered at him and stoned him, and Zechariah, at his death, prayed for God's judgment. So God intervened and caused Hazael king of Aram to attack him; after he captured Gath, he advanced toward Jerusalem. This was a chastening from the Lord because of the evil of Joash.

12.11.3.en: From this the weakness of Joash's character appears: he lived with God because of the guidance of Jehoiada, but after his death he was led, on the counsel of the princes of Judah, to the worship of idols.

12.11.4.en: Be steady in your relationship with God, committed to a spiritual rule that does not waver, even if circumstances take you away from your father or your spiritual guide. Do not be shaken, but persevere in your striving and trust in the help of God, which will support you.

12.12.0.en: Jehoash wanted to spare Jerusalem the destruction and ruin that was about to befall it when Hazael invaded it, so he decided to bribe him with money. He took all that his fathers had dedicated for the service of the sanctuary, what Jehoshaphat, Jehoram and Ahaziah had offered, as well as all the gold kept in the treasuries of the Temple and the treasuries of the royal palace, and handed it to Hazael, who accepted it as the price of his turning back from invading Jerusalem; that is, he gave him all the gold and silver found in the house of the Lord.

12.12.1.en: We notice that Joash, as a result of his neglect of the worship of God, did not think to take refuge in Him to rescue him from the hand of Hazael. He relied on his own mind in offering the money, though it was not his own money but the money of God. And God allowed Hazael to withdraw from Jerusalem out of regard for the goodness of Joash in his earlier life, in the days of Jehoiada; that is, He was content with a limited chastening of Joash. He also chastened him with many diseases (2 Chr 24:25). And so Joash became weak, unable to resist his enemies, and afflicted with diseases, because he had departed from God and lost His support.

12.13.0.en: The rest of the acts of Joash and all the events of the period of his reign are written in “the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah,” which is not the Book of Chronicles found in the Holy Bible.

12.14.0.en: The end of Joash was a tragic end, for some of his men rose up against him and killed him in “the house of Millo,” which Solomon had built, as Joash was going down by the road leading to the city of Silla.

12.15.0.en: Jozachar the son of Shimeath: he is the same as Zabad in (2 Chr 24:26), the son of an Ammonite woman, and one of the two who took part in the assassination of Joash.

12.15.1.en: Jehozabad the son of Shomer: one of the men of Joash who killed him.

12.15.2.en: Two of his men assassinated him, Jozachar the son of Shimeath and Jehozabad the son of Shomer. He was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Amaziah reigned after him.

12.15.3.en: Here we find the end of one who begins well and then turns away from God. He did not meet only troubles, but his two servants betrayed him and killed him; for if the king is far from God, worshiping idols, so too his servants easily become idolaters with no principles, and so they kill the king. And because of his turning away from God he was not buried in the tombs of the kings, but was buried only in the city of David. All this was vengeance and chastening from God for the blood of Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, the innocent.

12.15.4.en: The reign of Jehoahaz, then of his son Joash (1) The reign of Jehoahaz over Israel (vv. 1-9)

12.15.5.en: 1- In the three and twentieth year of Joash the son of Ahaziah king of Judah Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned seventeen years. 2- And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin; he departed not therefrom. 3- And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria, and into the hand of Benhadad the son of Hazael, all their days. 4- And Jehoahaz besought the LORD, and the LORD hearkened unto him: for he saw the oppression of Israel, because the king of Syria oppressed them. 5- (And the LORD gave Israel a saviour, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians: and the children of Israel dwelt in their tents, as beforetime. 6- Nevertheless they departed not from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, who made Israel sin, but walked therein: and there remained the grove also in Samaria.) 7- Neither did he leave of the people to Jehoahaz but fifty horsemen, and ten chariots, and ten thousand footmen; for the king of Syria had destroyed them, and had made them like the dust by threshing. 8- Now the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz, and all that he did, and his might, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? 9- And Jehoahaz slept with his fathers; and they buried him in Samaria: and Joash his son reigned in his stead.

13.0.s.en: (3) The bribing of the king of Aram and then the death of Joash

13.0.0.en: Jehoahaz the son of Jehu took the throne of Israel in the twenty-third year of Joash the son of Ahaziah king of Judah, in fulfillment of the Lord's promise to Jehu that his sons to the fourth generation would sit on the throne of Israel; and here the first generation begins its rule. The reign of Jehoahaz lasted seventeen years, and he was followed by Joash, then Jeroboam II, then his son Zechariah. In this the promise of God is fulfilled that the descendants of Jehu would reign to the fourth generation, which is the longest period that any royal house reigned in the kingdom of Israel. Jehoahaz is not mentioned in the Second Book of Chronicles, because that book concentrated on the kings of Judah, and Jehoahaz had no connection with the kings of Judah. It should be noted that he reigned seventeen years, and during the last three of them his son Joash shared the kingship with him. Many kings made their sons share the rule with them, to encourage them and so that no other person would seize the kingdom; for in the kingdom of Israel there was no obligation that the son inherit the kingship of his father, and so anyone could seize the kingdom.

13.0.1.en: It is mentioned (ch. 12:1) that Joash king of Judah began to reign in the seventh year of Jehu king of Israel, and it is also mentioned that Jehu reigned twenty-eight years (ch. 10:36), so that the end of the reign of Jehu and the accession of his son Jehoahaz came twenty-one years after the accession of Joash king of Judah. But what is mentioned here is that Jehoahaz began to reign in the twenty-third year of Joash king of Judah, and there is no contradiction, because part of a year is counted as a year. There is a part of a year before the twenty-first year and a part after the twenty-first year, so the total is twenty-three years. This is what the writer reckoned in this chapter, whereas in the other places we mentioned here, the writer did not count the parts of the year.

13.1.0.en: Jehoahaz walked in the sins of idolatry, which Jeroboam the son of Nebat, the first king of the kingdom of Israel, began, and in which, sadly, all the kings of Israel walked. These sins are summed up in:

13.1.1.en: 1- Bowing down to the idols that Jeroboam made in Bethel and Dan.

13.1.2.en: 2- Appointing priests who were not of the descendants of Aaron, to offer worship to these idols.

13.1.3.en: 3- Establishing feasts other than those prescribed by the Law of Moses (1 Kgs 12:28-33). And the remarkable thing is that at the very time when Jehoahaz begins to do these evils, Joash king of Judah, at the same time, that is in this same year, on the other side is occupied with repairing the house of the Lord.

13.1.4.en: Be zealous for the worship and honoring of God, however widespread evil becomes around you and however many follow it. And know that God not only rejoices in you and promises you the Kingdom, but also helps you and establishes you in the spiritual life, even if you are alone in the midst of many.

13.2.0.en: Benhadad: a name repeated among the kings of Aram; he was the commander of the army of his father Hazael, and then reigned after him, and that was after the death of Jehoahaz king of Israel.

13.2.1.en: The Lord was angry with Jehoahaz and the people of Israel because of their worship of idols, and so He allowed Hazael king of Aram and his son Benhadad to attack the kingdom of Israel, killing many, taking some of their cities and carrying some into captivity, until the kingdom was greatly distressed. And God did not fight for them, so that perhaps they might feel their weakness, repent and return to Him; but sadly they continued in the worship of idols.

13.3.0.en: Jehoahaz cried out to the Lord in supplication, and He answered his supplication, because He saw the troubles that His people were suffering under the dominion of the king of Aram. But He did not deliver them quickly, so that they might turn from the worship of idols, and God intervened and stopped the attack of the Arameans in the days of King Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz (v. 25).

13.3.1.en: Despite the turning away of Jehoahaz from the worship of the Lord, the Lord heard him, because He saw the affliction of His people, and the Scripture says, “In their affliction he was afflicted.” The Lord pays attention to any movement toward Him, however weak. God is found by the one who seeks Him, that perhaps he may complete his repentance and worship Him with all his heart.

13.4.0.en: God saved His people after the reign of Jehoahaz, in the days of his son Jehoash, when Assyria rose against Aram and weakened it. This helped Jehoash to recover the cities of Israel that had been seized, and the people returned to dwell in safety in their dwellings; that is, the war ended.

13.5.0.en: The grove: a tall pole set up on the high places for the worship of the moon, with altars built beside this pole.

13.5.1.en: Despite what the Lord had done for them, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, who led Israel into transgression, but continued in their evil ways, and the idol of Ashtoreth remained in Samaria. The first to set up such poles in Israel was King Ahab (1 Kgs 16:32, 33). It is understood from this verse that they walked in this worship, that is, they continued in what they were accustomed to of the worship of idols, provoking the Lord. And so we see that their seeking the mercy of God was so that they might enjoy His help, but they also continued in their evils and refused repentance, although God had saved them from their enemies for the purpose of their repentance and not for their own well-being.

13.6.0.en: There remained of the army of Jehoahaz only fifty horsemen, ten war chariots and ten thousand foot soldiers (they had been eight hundred thousand in the days of David), because the king of Aram had destroyed the army of Jehoahaz when he held sway over them before, and trampled them as dust is trampled.

13.7.0.en: The rest of what Jehoahaz did, and his excess in evil and the worship of idols, is written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. Jehoahaz died and they buried him with his fathers in Samaria, where tombs had been set apart in Samaria for the kings of Israel, and his son Joash took the throne after him.

13.7.1.en: (2) The reign of Jehoash over Israel (vv. 10-13)

13.7.2.en: 10- In the thirty and seventh year of Joash king of Judah began Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned sixteen years. 11- And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD; he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel sin: but he walked therein. 12- And the rest of the acts of Joash, and all that he did, and his might wherewith he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? 13- And Joash slept with his fathers; and Jeroboam sat upon his throne: and Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.

13.8.0.en: In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz ascended the throne of Israel, the second generation of the dynasty of Jehu. He reigned in Samaria sixteen years, and he reigned with his father Jehoahaz for three years, and then his father died.

13.8.1.en: The kings of Judah and Israel in the days of Joash king of Judah.

13.8.2.en: Kings of Judah, years, kings of Israel: Joash king of Judah began to reign; the command to repair the Temple, 23; Jehoahaz king of Israel began to reign; 37; Jehoash king of Israel began to reign with his father Jehoahaz; Amaziah king of Judah began to reign; 40; the death of Jehoahaz and Joash reigns alone over Israel.

13.9.0.en: Joash too was a wicked ruler; he did not withdraw from the crooked ways in which Jeroboam the son of Nebat walked, and he led the people after him in these same ways.

13.9.1.en: Leadership is very important and its influence is great, for the wicked kings led their peoples astray. So be careful in your leadership of those around you, whether you are a father or a servant, so that you lead everyone in the way of God, and do not forget that you are the light of the world and the salt of the earth.

13.10.0.en: The rest of the acts of Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz, his excess in evil and the details of his war against Amaziah king of Judah, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. But there was something of goodness in Joash, because he turned to Elisha the prophet, as will appear from the following verses, and he regarded him as a man of God, and this has value in the eyes of God, and perhaps this is what made God grant deliverance from Aram in his days.

13.11.0.en: Joash died and was buried with his fathers in Samaria with the kings of Israel, and his son Jeroboam sat on the throne of Israel after him, the third generation of the descendants of Jehu.

13.11.1.en: (3) Elisha prophesies the smiting of Aram (vv. 14-19)

13.11.2.en: 14- Now Elisha was fallen sick of his sickness whereof he died. And Joash the king of Israel came down unto him, and wept over his face, and said, O my father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof. 15- And Elisha said unto him, Take bow and arrows. And he took unto him bow and arrows. 16- And he said to the king of Israel, Put thine hand upon the bow. And he put his hand upon it: and Elisha put his hands upon the king’s hands. 17- And he said, Open the window eastward. And he opened it. Then Elisha said, Shoot. And he shot. And he said, The arrow of the LORD’S deliverance, and the arrow of deliverance from Syria: for thou shalt smite the Syrians in Aphek, till thou have consumed them. 18- And he said, Take the arrows. And he took them. And he said unto the king of Israel, Smite upon the ground. And he smote thrice, and stayed. 19- And the man of God was wroth with him, and said, Thou shouldest have smitten five or six times; then hadst thou smitten Syria till thou hadst consumed it: whereas now thou shalt smite Syria but thrice.

13.12.0.en: When Joash king of Israel learned of Elisha’s illness and his approaching death (Elisha was then eighty years old), Joash hurried to him and was deeply moved by the nearness of his departure, and he began to weep beside him until his tears fell on Elisha’s face, and perhaps he was kissing him in great grief. He called to him, “My father, my father,” declaring his submission to him, and he proclaimed to him the well-known words that Elisha had said to Elijah, that he was the chariot of Israel and its horsemen, that is, that he was the true power in the kingdom of Israel, because he was the man of God and his voice. But this passing emotional feeling does not accord with the whole life of Joash, for he walked in evil and worshiped idols.

13.13.0.en: Elisha said to him, “Take bow and arrows,” and he did so. Then he said to him, “Put your hand upon the bow,” and he drew the bow.

13.13.1.en: And Elisha put his hand upon the king’s hand, as a sign of the work of God in the war and the victory.

13.13.2.en: Of course the king’s guards had arrows and bows with them; he took them from them and did as Elisha commanded him. The obedience of the king appears in his submission to Elisha. His obedience represents human striving, while the hand of Elisha upon the king’s hand represents the grace and power of God, which support those who obey the commandments of God.

13.13.3.en: And here we see that God uses visual aids in conveying His prophecy to the king through the mouth of Elisha, in order to confirm the prophecy and fix it in the heart and faith of the king, as He did with many prophets, such as Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and He uses them with us through the events of our life, that we may know Him and walk with Him.

13.13.4.en: God had promised Elijah (1 Kgs 19:17) that whoever escaped the sword of Hazael Jehu would slay, and whoever escaped the sword of Jehu Elisha would slay. Although Elisha did not kill anyone, he points in this verse to the sword of the word of God in the hand of Elisha, with which he rebuked the wicked and led all to repentance, whether kings and princes or the people. The sword of Elisha also appears in his support of the kings with the power of God and in the smiting of their enemies, as he supported Jehoshaphat (ch. 3:18) in the smiting of Moab, and as he supported Joash in the smiting of Aram, as appears in this verse.

13.13.5.en: You must do your duty in spiritual striving against sin and for the acquiring of every virtue, so that you may enjoy the help and support of God, and take care to keep His commandments and obey them, and then His grace will support you.

13.14.0.en: Aphek: a city east of the Jordan, the same as modern Aphek, which is also called Afiq. It lies five kilometers east of the Sea of Galilee.

13.14.1.en: Then he said to him, “Open the window eastward,” and he opened it, because the Arameans, the enemies of Israel, dwell to the east of them. And Elisha said, “Shoot,” and he shot the arrow, and Elisha said, “The arrow of the LORD’s deliverance, the arrow of victory over Aram, for you shall smite Aram in Aphek and make an end of them.” It was well known in war that the commander of the army would shoot an arrow into the midst of the city, and the soldiers would move to battle; and the meaning of this is that Joash’s shooting of the arrow, in obedience to Elisha, meant a declaration of war on Aram. This is the first lesson that Elisha taught Joash, that is, obedience to God and confidence that God will not leave him; as for the second lesson, it comes in the next two verses.

13.15.0.en: Then Elisha said, “Take the arrows,” and he took them, and Elisha said to the king, “Smite upon the ground,” and he smote upon the ground three times, and then stopped.

13.15.1.en: It appears from this that the king understood from the previous verse that he would be victorious over Aram, and so the striking of the arrows on the ground meant the smiting of Aram; he struck three times only and stopped, and this means the following:

13.15.2.en: 1- The king’s limited faith in the power of God, which would support him in smiting Aram and gaining victory over it; for he did not strike many arrows, but stopped striking quickly.

13.15.3.en: 2- The weakness of his zeal in resisting the enemies to the end, that is, his lack of effort to crush and destroy them. Perhaps there was some slackness in his heart, or he feared that Assyria would make war on him if he destroyed Aram, that is, that Assyria would fear Joash and so fight him and destroy him; or perhaps he wanted two opposing powers, Aram and Assyria, to remain so as to ensure some security. These were human thoughts and a weakness of reliance on God. And this is the second lesson that Elisha wanted to teach the king, which is to strive with all one’s strength, believing in the supporting grace of God, and so to gain complete victory; for according to the measure of one’s striving one receives power from God.

13.16.0.en: Elisha was angry with Joash and said, If you had struck five or six times, you would have made an end of Aram until they were completely destroyed; but now you will continue your victories over them only three times.

13.16.1.en: God wanted to save His people with a complete salvation, but Joash was unwilling to do what was needed to achieve that. Is not the conduct of Joash like that of those who content themselves with the very least in their spiritual relationship with the Lord, ignoring the means of spiritual growth, unwilling to strive to climb the ladder of the virtues?

13.16.2.en: (4) The bones of Elisha bring a dead man to life (vv. 20, 21)

13.16.3.en: 20- And Elisha died, and they buried him. And the bands of the Moabites invaded the land at the coming in of the year.

13.16.4.en: 21- And it came to pass, as they were burying a man, that, behold, they spied a band of men; and they cast the man into the sepulchre of Elisha: and when the man was let down, and touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.

13.17.0.en: At the coming in of the year: that is, after a year had passed since the death of Elisha, or it may mean that the Moabites used to attack the kingdom of Israel at the beginning of every year.

13.17.1.en: Elisha died and was buried, and that was in the year 834 B.C., that is, at the end of the ninth century B.C., and the Church celebrates the feast of his departure on the twentieth of Paoni. It happened at that time, a year after the death of Elisha, that Moab invaded the land of Israel.

13.17.2.en: This shows the weakness of the kingdom of Israel, for the peoples around it made war on it and penetrated deep into its land.

13.17.3.en: And we notice that after the death of Elisha the Moabites invade Israel and their invasions are repeated, and this shows that the power of God that was in Elisha had left the people, so that they were exposed to many attacks by enemies, because protection had been removed from them. And despite the promise of God of victory over Aram, we find other enemies, the Moabites, attacking the land. This means the need to be on guard against all the enemies who can fight us from different directions, and not against a single enemy or a single sin.

13.18.0.en: While the Jews were carrying a dead man to bury him, they were surprised by the Moabites attacking their land, so they threw the dead man into the nearest grave they came upon and fled. This grave was the grave of Elisha, and when the body of the dead man touched the bones of Elisha, he received power from God, which raised him alive, so that God might show His power in His saints even after their death. And here we see Elisha raising a dead man in his lifetime, the son of the Shunammite, and after his death in this incident. By this Elisha is a type of Christ, who raised the dead while He was on earth, and by His death saves us and raises us from the death of sin and gives us eternal life.

13.18.1.en: And the raising of this dead man after the death of Elisha and his parting from his people proclaims hope to the people that God is able to raise them, if they worship Him and obey the words of His prophets.

13.18.2.en: And as God honored Elijah by his ascent to heaven, so also He showed the greatness of Elisha by raising a dead man by the touch of his bones after his death, and this is clear evidence of the intercession of the saints.

13.18.3.en: The raising of a dead man by the bones of a dead man is the only incident of this kind in the Holy Bible, and it proclaims the following:

13.18.4.en: 1- A reminder to the people of the words of Elisha, that they might obey him and submit to God.

13.18.5.en: 2- That God is present in the midst of His people, even after the death of His prophets, and is ready to act, if the people submit to Him.

13.18.6.en: The bodies of the saints are a great blessing; they remind us of their lives and urge us to imitate them, relying on their prayers for us. So take care to befriend the saints and to receive the blessing of their bodies, that they may help you in your spiritual striving.

13.18.7.en: (5) Hazael oppresses the king of Israel (vv. 22-25)

13.18.8.en: 22- But Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz. 23- And the LORD was gracious unto them, and had compassion on them, and had respect unto them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them, neither cast he them from his presence as yet. 24- So Hazael king of Syria died; and Benhadad his son reigned in his stead.

13.18.9.en: 25- And Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again out of the hand of Benhadad the son of Hazael the cities, which he had taken out of the hand of Jehoahaz his father by war. Three times did Joash beat him, and recovered the cities of Israel.

13.19.0.en: Returning to verse 3 of this chapter and Hazael’s oppression of the children of Israel in the days of Jehoahaz, and verse 5, in which the Lord gave Israel a saviour who freed them from the dominion of Hazael; this saviour was Joash the son of Jehoahaz.

13.19.1.en: Here the description of the situation in which the children of Israel were, and the Lord’s deliverance of them, is repeated.

13.19.2.en: Hazael king of Aram oppressed Israel throughout the reign of Jehoahaz. And because the Lord is compassionate and gracious toward His people, He was distressed at their distress, as the Scripture says, “In all their affliction he was afflicted.” The Lord remembered His covenant with their fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and was unwilling to destroy them until that time, or to cast them away. And He did not let Hazael annihilate them. But when they persisted in evil, He was compelled to allow them to be taken captive by Assyria, and that was about a hundred years later.

13.20.0.en: Hazael king of Aram died, and his son Benhadad sat on the throne of Aram after him.

13.21.0.en: Joash the son of Jehoahaz recovered the Israelite cities that Hazael had taken in war. Three battles took place between Joash and Benhadad, in all of which Joash was victorious, and he was able to impose his control over those cities again. By this the word of Elisha was fulfilled, when he saw that he had struck only three arrows to the ground, and said to him that he would smite Aram only three times and would not destroy them.

13.21.1.en: How does this king, who had turned away from the worship of the Lord, become an instrument for the salvation of his people? This is the work of grace. When a person humbles himself before God and a sign of repentance and contrition of heart appears in him, the Lord hastens to offer every help to pluck that soul out of the captivity of sin. Salvation is offered even to the most wretched and the most unworthy of people, so take courage, whatever your sins, and offer repentance, for God loves you and will receive you, and even work through you.

13.21.2.en: Amaziah and Azariah kings of Judah, and Joash and Jeroboam kings of Israel
